elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to synthesise evidence of the longitudinal associations between childhood and adolescent leisure-time physical activity on adulthood physical activity behaviours and health outcomes.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to synthesise evidence of the longitudinal associations between childhood and adolescent leisure-time physical activity on adulthood physical activity behaviours and health outcomes.
elements.reason: The main objective/review question is explicitly stated in the abstract.

elements.quote: English, peer-reviewed observational studies with a minimum of two timepoints of data collection were eligible for inclusion. We included studies that investigated the association between participation in leisure-time physical activity types in children and adolescents (i.e., 5-18 years), and physical activity, mental health, or cardiovascular outcomes in adulthood (i.e., ≥ 18 years).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the main eligibility (inclusion) criteria regarding language, publication type, design, population, and outcomes.

elements.quote: A systematic search of the literature was conducted across five databases from inception to July 2022.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the search date (July 2022) and number of databases, but does not name the information sources (databases) individually.
The abstract does not mention any risk of bias assessment methods (e.g., the modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale).
The abstract does not describe the methods used to present or synthesize results (e.g., narrative synthesis).

elements.quote: Fourteen studies were included in the review, totalling 34,388 observations across five countries.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included studies, participants/observations, and relevant characteristics (countries).

elements.quote: Running in adolescence was associated with increased adulthood physical activity in both sexes, while sports involvement was associated with an increase in physical activity in males only. Adolescent team sports participation was associated with reduced odds of early adulthood depression, with varying findings for anxiety disorders.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes (physical activity, depression, anxiety) by activity type.

elements.quote: Due to between-study heterogeneity in exposure and outcome measures, a metaanalysis was not feasible in this review
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted, so no summary estimate with confidence/credible interval is required in the abstract.

elements.quote: Running in adolescence was associated with increased adulthood physical activity in both sexes, while sports involvement was associated with an increase in physical activity in males only. Adolescent team sports participation was associated with reduced odds of early adulthood depression
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect for the compared groups (e.g., increased physical activity in both sexes vs males only; reduced odds of depression).
The abstract does not summarize limitations of the included evidence such as risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision.

elements.quote: Preliminary findings suggest that the lifelong behavioural and health benefits of adolescent participation in leisure-time physical activity appear to be related to the type of activity undertaken, with potential differences between sexes... these findings provide important insights for public health strategies to optimise lifelong health and physical activity participation.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications for public health.
The abstract does not state the primary source of funding for the review.

elements.quote: Prospero registration CRD42022347792.
elements.reason: The abstract provides the registry name (PROSPERO) and registration number.

elements.quote: Previous LTPA-focussed research has mostly been quantified by time, frequency, and/or intensity (e.g., light intensity, moderate-vigorous intensity), with little investigation into the impact of the specific activity types of LTPA being performed [12-15]. The World Health Organisation Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour Guidelines Development Group [14] identified understanding the health effects of different PA types as one of four major evidence gaps in current knowledge.
elements.reason: The Introduction describes the current state of knowledge (PA-LTPA research to date) and explicitly identifies uncertainties/evidence gaps, including the WHO-identified gap regarding health effects of different PA types.

elements.quote: Therefore, summarising the current state of knowledge of the longitudinal health and behavioural effects of specific LTPA types could help inform public health policy and direct future research... Such knowledge may assist in reducing the global burden of major diseases, including cardiovascular disease and mental health disorders, and further, achieving PA targets for improved population health.
elements.reason: The importance and need for the review are clearly explained in terms of public health burden, policy relevance, and directing future research.

elements.quote: Previous systematic reviews have highlighted the influence of activity structure and type on psychosocial outcomes in children [22] and cardiovascular health in adults [23]. Another review identified a largely positive relationship between overall childhood sport participation and adulthood PA [24]. However, the longitudinal associations between participation in specific LTPA types during childhood and adolescence and adult health and PA behaviours remains unknown.
elements.reason: Existing similar systematic reviews are cited and the need for the current review is explained by identifying what those reviews did not address (specific LTPA types and longitudinal adult outcomes).
This is a review of associations between LTPA types and later outcomes, not a review of intervention effects, so no proposed mechanism of intervention action is required.
The review examines exposure-outcome associations in observational longitudinal studies, not a complex intervention or delivery context, so a logic model is not required.

None of the retrieved evidence contains an explicit statement of the review objective(s) or question(s) framed using a question-formulation framework. The title implies the topic, and eligibility criteria (text_4) hint at the focus, but no explicit objectives statement is reported in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: observational study design on humans with at least two timepoints of data collection; ... measurement of at least one specific type of LTPA ... in childhood or adolescence ... quantitative assessment of at least one mental health outcome ... cardiovascular health outcome ... or PA outcome in adulthood
elements.reason: This is a review of observational/prospective longitudinal studies of exposure (types of LTPA) and later outcomes, not a review of intervention effects; therefore planned intervention comparisons in PICO format do not apply.
